criterion_notes.c1: Examines household drinking-water service access in six rural communities in Northwest Cameroon, comparing private piped yard connections, communal stand taps, and unimproved sources (streams, springs, and wells).
criterion_notes.c2: Passes BOTH the plain wording of Criterion 2 and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading. Under the plain reading, the study examines decentralized community-based water management (CBWM), water management committees (WMCs), CBOs, traditional chiefdom governance, and rural exclusion from centralized urban utilities (CAMWATER and CDE) under the 1998 water law. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, rather than merely describing generic self-help project delivery, the study empirically examines concrete rule-type mechanisms directly governing household service access: (1) tariff and cost-recovery rules plus connection-eligibility rules set by WMCs (mandatory gender- and age-differentiated capital contributions, an upfront cash requirement determining eligibility for a private connection, and tiered monthly maintenance fees of 2 USD for private connections versus 1 USD for communal taps); (2) enforcement mechanisms including supply termination for non-payment and customary sanctions imposed by village chiefs (heavy fines and denial of authorization to perform funeral rites for non-contributors); and (3) institutional service-provision structure excluding rural areas from state utilities.
criterion_notes.c3: Contains primary empirical evidence from a structured household questionnaire survey administered to 108 household heads (18 per village across 6 villages sampled from a frame of 180 households), reported in descriptive statistical tables (Tables 1-3).
criterion_notes.c4: Reports multiple direct household access outcomes: share with private piped water connection (34%) versus communal stand taps (66%), per-capita daily water consumption (35.6 l/c/d for private connections vs. 24.7 l/c/d for communal taps), walking distance (mean 350 m) and daily collection time (mean 71.6 min/day), affordability barriers (71 communal-tap households unable to afford connection fees; 54% unable to regularly pay the 1 USD monthly fee), and supply termination.
criterion_notes.c5: Population and unit of analysis (households; N = 108 across 6 rural villages in 3 districts of Northwest Cameroon), exposure (CBWM institutional structure and WMC cost-recovery, upfront connection-fee eligibility, and enforcement rules), outcome (connection type, daily per-capita consumption, distance/time, affordability exclusion, and disconnection), and study design (cross-sectional multi-village household questionnaire survey) are all clearly identifiable.

study_design: Cross-sectional multi-village household survey using structured questionnaires
population_and_sample: Households (unit of analysis: household) in six rural villages (Njimkang, Ngarum, Muloin, Baicham, Tugi, and Zang-Tabi) across three rural districts (Mbengwi, Njinikom, and Ndu) in Northwest Cameroon; sample of 108 households (18 household questionnaires per village drawn from a population list of 180 households).
exposure: Community-based water management (CBWM) institutional governance and water management committee (WMC) cost-recovery, eligibility, and enforcement rules (mandatory gender/age-differentiated capital contributions, upfront cash requirement for private connection eligibility, tiered monthly maintenance tariffs of 2 USD for private connections vs. 1 USD for communal taps, supply termination, and village-chief fines/funeral-rite sanctions) in rural areas excluded from urban state utilities (CAMWATER and CDE).
outcome: Household piped water connection type (private yard connection [34%] vs. public stand tap [66%] vs. reliance on streams/springs), daily water consumption per household and per capita (35.6 l/c/d vs. 24.7 l/c/d), walking distance (mean 350 m) and daily collection time (mean 71.6 min/day), inability to afford upfront connection fees (71 households) or monthly fees (54%), and supply termination.
rationale: Full-text empirical household survey (N = 108 households across 6 villages in Northwest Cameroon) examining rural household drinking-water access under community-based water management (CBWM) in areas unserved by centralized urban state utilities. Beyond general CBWM project mobilization, the paper empirically examines concrete rule-type mechanisms governing service access under the 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 clarification: WMC upfront cash eligibility requirements for private yard connections, obligatory gender/age-graduated capital contributions, tiered monthly maintenance tariffs ($2/month for private connections vs. $1/month for public stand taps), supply termination for non-payment, and customary chief-imposed fines and funeral-rite bans, linking these rules to household exclusion from private connections, affordability barriers, water quantity consumed (l/c/d), and collection distance/time. Meets all inclusion criteria (c1-c6).
